analysis.one_liner: Lets insurers sell short-term and association health plans that skip Affordable Care Act protections.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee in February 2021, never received a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law the rules for two kinds of health coverage that sit outside most Affordable Care Act requirements: short-term plans that can be bought for just under a year, and association health plans that let small businesses or self-employed people band together to buy group coverage. The bill would require insurers to renew short-term coverage at the enrollee's option, but those plans could still avoid rules like covering preexisting conditions. It also includes a provision shielding franchisors and associations from being treated as the legal employer of workers in their plans. The bill was referred to House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, healthier people, self-employed workers, and small businesses would have gained access to cheaper plans with skinnier benefits, and insurers selling these plans would have gained a federally protected market. Franchisors and trade associations would have gained a shield from joint-employer liability when they sponsor coverage for franchise and member workers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers selling skimpy plans; self-employed buyers

how_it_helps.text: Lets short-term, limited-duration insurance contracts run just under 12 months (not counting extensions) and stay exempt from certain Affordable Care Act market rules, such as covering people with preexisting conditions.
Requires issuers of short-term plans to renew or continue that coverage at the option of the enrollee, giving buyers some continuity.

Lets groups or associations of employers sponsor fully insured group health plans as if they were employers, including self-employed 'working owners,' with rules barring discrimination based on health factors for membership or premiums.
Provides that participating in or facilitating an association plan does not create an employer or joint-employer relationship under federal or state law, including for franchisors and franchisees.

analysis.who_pays: People with preexisting conditions and anyone who stays in ACA-compliant coverage would bear higher costs as healthier buyers move to cheaper exempt plans, shrinking the risk pool that keeps ACA premiums down. Enrollees in the exempt plans would bear the risk of uncovered medical bills, since those plans can skip required benefits and preexisting-condition coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sick enrollees and ACA marketplace customers

drawbacks.text: Short-term plans under the bill remain exempt from Affordable Care Act market requirements, such as coverage of individuals with preexisting conditions, so buyers can be left without coverage exactly when they get sick.

Because these plans would be authorized in statute and cheaper than ACA-compliant coverage, healthier people would tend to leave ACA-compliant pools, which pushes premiums up for those who remain — particularly people with health conditions.

The bill's nondiscrimination rules for association plans are narrower than the full set of Affordable Care Act market rules; plans must avoid discrimination on health factors but do not have to cover the essential benefits ACA plans must cover.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real benefit here: self-employed people and small businesses often face very high premiums, and cheaper options plus guaranteed renewability would help some of them. But the way the bill gets to lower prices is by removing protections, and the cost lands on the people least able to bear it — those with preexisting conditions face both exclusion from the cheap plans and higher premiums in the plans that remain. A renewal guarantee for short-term plans is a small consumer protection bolted onto a framework whose main effect is expanding coverage that can deny or exclude sick people.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and a health subcommittee in February 2021, no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Budd introduced the FLEX Act in the House on February 3, 2021, joined by Rep. Andy Harris.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee on the day of introduction.
On February 4, 2021, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health.
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People with preexisting conditions and ACA marketplace enrollees are better off, since the exemption from ACA rules was never written into law. Insurers who would have sold the exempt plans lost the new market the bill would have created.

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the February 2021 referral; the bill went to the Health Subcommittee and was never brought to a markup or vote.

against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after the February 2021 referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had two Republican sponsors and no recorded floor vote or roll call, so no partisan split on its merits was ever measured; it died in committee without recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Health insurers selling short-term and association plans
industries.note: The bill would give statutory authority to plans that sit outside Affordable Care Act rules, creating a federally protected market for skinnier coverage. Those plans profit by charging less to healthy buyers while not covering preexisting conditions, and the cost of sicker enrollees shifts to ACA-compliant pools.

The bill would bar association health plan participation from creating a joint-employer relationship, a liability shield for franchise chains and associations that sponsor coverage for members' and franchisees' workers. Workers would get coverage through entities that are not their legal employer.

Cheaper exempt plans would pull healthier customers out of ACA-compliant pools, raising per-person costs for the remaining, on-average sicker enrollment. Insurers and enrollees in the regulated market share an interest in keeping that from happening.
